utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. We are a bit late because the other case overran a little. We'll maybe buy five minutes at the end of the day, but let's see where we stand at that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are getting close to the end of your evidence, Mr. Vukovic. Please remember that the solemn declaration to speak the truth continues to apply today and your cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will now continue. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, the first thing I wanted to ask you about is a document from your battalion which is a log-book of outgoing telegrams and this is Exhibit P2010. And you were asked about this when you testified in the Milosevic case; at page 46038 Mr. Nice pointed out to you that that outgoing telegram book has a single entry for the 19th of February, 1999, and then there are no further entries until the 20th of April. And he asked you where were the missing documents. Your answer at the bottom of that page was: "You can notice that there are some pages missing. I've already said that my office at the barracks was directly hit and that most of or the largest portion of the documents for 1998 were destroyed. As a result of those NATO strikes that a large number of documents were destroyed. Truth to tell, I'm surprised that this has remained." Is it still your position and your explanation for those missing pages in your outgoing telegram log that they were destroyed by the bombing?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a telegram log that we're talking about. It's probably a different kind of document. As far as I remember, this register, telegram log, was an internal one, the one that I had, because a combined log was kept by the brigade, it was preserved and filed away. I'm trying to remember exactly what Mr. Nice asked me at the time, and I think it was in reference to combat reports -- operations reports actually and there were internal notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... shown one because otherwise we're going to have 15 minutes of an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, if we could go to the next page in both the English and the B/C/S. We'll have a rotate 90 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is the first entry in that outgoing telegram log, it's from the 19th of February. Seeing that document, does that help you understand what I'm asking you about?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go one more page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see the next entry in the log is for the 20th of April. Mr. Nice asked you about the missing pages, and your explanation was as I said, you suggested that it was because of the NATO strikes and that documents were destroyed. Is that still your explanation for why there are no telegrams in this log between 19 February 1999 and 20 April?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think your understanding of my answer is entirely erroneous, the answer that I provided to Mr. Nice at the time. I said that as a result of the air-strikes the majority of the documents had been destroyed, but this is not a log, this is not a combat document. This is a notebook that was kept internally at my signal centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. That was your answer when you testified under oath in Milosevic. My question is: Is that still your answer or do you want to change it and tell us that you were mistaken when you gave that answer in Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have an accurate quote from the Milosevic trial. My impression is the witness is persistently trying to explain but Mr. Hannis will not grant him a chance to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis quoted word for word as I understand it from page 46038. Are you saying that that's inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't have that page in front of me. I'm listening to the answers, I'm listening to the questions, and I feel there's some sort of a discrepancy at work here or -- of course it might always be an interpretation problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to be either. The quotation was word for word, so please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you need me to read your answer from Milosevic again or do you recall what I read?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, what is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to make myself useful. Perhaps Mr. Nice's question should be read out as well not just the answer, and then perhaps we'll be in the picture, as it were. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If Mr. Cepic wants to add to what happens here, he can do it in re-examination. There's nothing wrong with the approach Mr. Hannis is taking. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope all this is not coming out of my 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you need me to read your answer again?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I abide fully by the answer that I provided at the time; however, I talked with Mr. Nice about the insufficiencies of this document for at least 20 minutes. I think, to the extent that I can now remember, he asked a minimum of ten questions about this very document. Your quote, I don't know what the specific question was for that quote, and if I may just be given a chance to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody here appears to be thinking that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not everything was copied here, but then again I have to say that this was an internal document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, this document has an entry on the 19th of February and the next entry is not until the 20th of April. It's described as a log-book of outgoing telegrams. Why is there nothing in it between the 19th of February and the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, one of the explanations is precisely this: Some of the documents were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's your testimony that the missing pages between the 19th of February and the 20th of April were destroyed in the NATO bombing but the other pages were left intact; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's no -- but please again you're twisting my words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... unless it's something to do with interpretation or something, but I get the impression that there's an effort being made here to spoil the cross-examination, which seems perfectly legitimate on the basis of the material being used, and this is the fourth intervention in this cross-examination in about five minutes of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honour, just, just the interpretation. Mr. Hannis is reading this log-book and the Serbian translation should be a notebook, whereas it's being translated as a log or register, that's the interpretation that I'm receiving in the B/C/S and that is one thing that I was trying to draw your attention to, no more than that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's also what is said in the written document itself, to which no one has so far taken exception. So please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me address that. I'm going to go to page 46038, I'll start with your answer at line 15: "There were many log-books of incoming and outgoing telegrams. They were kept in 1998 as well." So you're the one using the term "log-books." Mr. Nice's question at line 17 was: "Where's the one that covers the period the 25th of March and until the beginning of April because all we have for outgoing -- I beg your pardon, for incoming is something that starts on the 26th of April, and all we have for outgoing is a single entry for the 19th of February and then entries for the 20th of April. So where are the ones that cover the period in which we are particularly interested, the 25th of March to the end of March, where are they?" Your answer: "Well, had you let me finish I would have told you that too. If you look you can notice that there is some pages missing, and I've already said that my office at the barracks was directly hit and that most of -- or the largest portion of the documents for 1998 were destroyed. The command post was hit with a direct hit three times, and among other things it was during that action, NATO strikes to be precise, it was during that, as a result of those NATO strikes, that a large number of documents were destroyed." Mr. Nice says: "Finally" -- And you say: "To tell you the truth to tell, I'm surprised that this has remained." Now, that was your answer and you told me earlier that you stick by that answer, right? That's still your answer today about why those pages are missing? Can you say yes or no to that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Major Mancic, was he in your -- under your command?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Major Mancic was not under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You know about his prosecution for crimes -- for war crimes against civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was prosecuted. I know that he was convicted for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you testified in some of those proceedings, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was just that once before the Nis military court, and the other time was before the district court in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In 1998 do you recall what the radio code-name or call-sign that you used for your 2nd Battalion or for Battle Group 2, was it Koritnik?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the communications work-plan contained all the call-signs for all participants, but this changed very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Koritnik, I can't remember. I used to be Vihor for a time. Most frequently we were, when I say "we," I mean members of the 549th Motorised Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Poljanica, but we did have another number, so it's possible yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to go into private session for a couple of questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, we shall go into private session. [Private session].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh. Sorry, Mr. Haider.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first thing I wanted to ask you about was your conviction that Mr. Cepic asked you about when you first started testifying. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before you came into court that day, that evening, to begin testifying in this case, did anyone tell you that your conviction had been mentioned or discussed in open court with the earlier witness?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one's ever told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So you weren't surprised when it first was brought up?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, yes, I was, because this is not something that I had previous discussed, at least as far as I remember, with Counsel Cepic. Anyway, it's been over three or four years since I was convicted. It should have been expunged a long time ago, but this never materialized. That's why I never mentioned that because I believe that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we look at Exhibit P3083. Colonel, I tell you this is your personnel file that we received pursuant to a request, and I think it's at page 97 of the B/C/S, but I think maybe it will be easiest if I have the usher assist me in handing you a hard copy of the pages I'm most interested in. This is a document from the military court in Nis dated the 21st of November, 2003, and it's the judgement in your case. Do you recognise that? Did you ever see it before?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it, that's the conviction. Let me just see if it's there in its entirety. This was delivered to me at my home address because I had already retired by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. When you were asked about this at page 21329, beginning at line 18, in part of your answer you said that: "Now, as to how a criminal complaint came to be written, I don't know. I have no information concerning that." You didn't mean to say that you didn't understand what you were accused of; you understood that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I understood that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood what I was accused of. I just don't know how this first started.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could go to page 2 of the B/C/S and it's also on page 2 of the English. I'll read a portion of that, Colonel. It says: "The accused, Vlatko Vukovic, as an official, commander of a battalion on undetermined day in February 2000 incited Radisa Vukadinovic to originate a false official document and use it as true by ordering Vukadinovic after he complained he had a deficit of 300 litres of diesel fuel to enter false data in the vehicle log sheets for the vehicles from this unit showing that the said had consumed around 30 litres of fuel each, thus justifying a deficit, and Vukadinovic did that." That's what happened, isn't it? You admitted that, right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the indictment says; however, one must read the statement of reasons for this to become clear, the accusations as well as the eventual conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm going to that. If you could go to page 3 in the B/C/S, and in the English it begins at the bottom of page 3. Let me read this and ask you another question. "Speaking their mind at the hearing about the indictment, both accused confessed. Vukovic pointed out that it was a clear case of discrepancy between the bookkeeping records and actual status of the received and consumed fuel in the unit at the time he was Commander-in-Chief. Otherwise, he's not questioning his behaviour described in this judgement." We're on to page 4 of the English now. "Confessing that he ordered the accused Vukadinovic, his subordinate, and the clerk in the unit to adjust this discrepancy and virtual dissipation by entering the subject amount of fuel into the vehicle log sheet for few vehicles." That's correct, isn't it? You admitted that you did do that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He has to wait for the translation, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you talked about this but you didn't actually read it. But for the most part it's what I told the judge, the trial judge. And this sentence clearly states that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could go to the bottom of your page 3 and in English I'm reading from about six lines down on page 5. Colonel, you'll see a couple lines up from the bottom of page 3 in B/C/S: "Therefore, the accused were undoubtedly aware of their doing and they did what they did on purpose. First the accused Vukovic being the commander knows, regardless of his assertion that such a practice existed elsewhere, that the subordinates must not be incited to commit a crime, that is, to concoct false documents" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please move the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- "or to enter untrue information into existing official documents." That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me that, whether it's correct or not or are you making a statement? I didn't understand. What is your question, actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says. Do you disagree that you were aware what you were doing and that you did it on purpose?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew full well what was going on in my unit. However, my superior commander knew it full well too and he ordered me to do that. I can tell you the story once again, the one that I told the judge, but I'm afraid that it's a bit lengthy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, maybe your --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only natural, sir, for you to understand why I did this, 1.800 soldiers needed to take a bath after three month --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of war. I did not have--

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop. You've answered my question. Mr. Cepic can follow-up if he wants to. You answered my question. Now, the point of this is you have said in this case that K89, a protected witness, is a liar; that K90, a protected witness, is a liar; that Merita Deda and Lizane Malaj from Korenica are liars; and in the Milosevic case you called Mr. Nice a liar at page 46133. And my suggestion to you, sir, is that you're the liar --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the objection, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear this witness say that Merita Deda and other witnesses are liars. I did not hear him use those words. I think that these are grave statements, insults, and the response to Nice and the mode of communication in the Milosevic trial, that's a different story altogether and the questions that were put by Mr. Nice, the standard of trial in the Milosevic case. Of course I'm not authorised to comment on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What were you going to say about the standard of trial in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, their way in which the Prosecutor, Mr. Nice, examined some Defence witnesses, cross-examined them, and the words that were addressed to them. That is the only thing that I wanted to point out, thank you, not the way in which the proceedings were conducted, but I was speaking in terms of the way in which counsel for the Prosecution addressed witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If the Bench had been unhappy about that, the Bench would have taken action about it, Mr. Cepic, so your criticism is of the Bench and that may be something that you are entitled to express if it leads to any particular conclusion. Now, we're only interested at this stage in one thing that was said by Mr. Nice, so what is your point in relation to the question that Mr. Hannis is asking rather than your widespread criticism of the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is not criticism of what the Trial Chamber did, not at all. As a matter of fact, I have full respect, great respect, of everything that the Trial Chamber did. However, as a professional I have certain objections vis-a-vis some of the cross-examinations conducted by counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Nice, in the proceedings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to repeat your general criticism of Mr. Nice or the proceedings. I am asking you: What is your objection to the point that Mr. Hannis is making about Mr. Nice's question in the trial? That's all. The rest of it we can live with, cope with, debate forever, and it will not make any difference to my approach to this that you appear to be critical of the part played by the Bench in the Milosevic trial; it's irrelevant to this case. But your particular criticism of what Mr. Nice is quoted as saying on that occasion is what I'm concerned about. What is your criticism?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these words that the Prosecutor used when speaking to the witness, saying that everybody was lying, I think that such words and such terms were not used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, I am at the moment, unless you can show me a quotation to the contrary or a misrepresentation, am prepared to accept what Mr. Hannis has said, that Mr. Vukovic in the Milosevic trial called Geoffrey Nice a liar. Now, what is your objection to the fact that he's putting that to the witness in the context of this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, Your Honour - and of course there is the transcript, so if I'm making a mistake, it's my mistake and I apologise for it - I think that previously during the course of this testimony Prosecutor Geoffrey Nice called the witness a liar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may be so. What's wrong with that in the system we're operating? I appreciate that in your own jurisdiction that may not be an appropriate way of proceeding, but you know very well that it's an acceptable way of proceeding here. I have my reservations about it too, but there's no basis for objecting because people use these expressions. They're simply putting their case and inviting the person to whom the point is made to comment, giving him an opportunity to answer the allegation in fairness to him. Now, what's happened here effectively is that there is no point in Mr. Hannis proceeding with that question. The witness -- we couldn't now have any regard to any answer the witness gives. He's going to have to think about whether he wants to formulate another question, but you should be very cautious about intervening in the way in which you have without, I would suggest, solid foundation in respect of any part of it. I quite concede that Mr. Vukovic has not said that Merita Deda was a liar. All that Mr. Hannis is saying the effect of his evidence is to suggest that she must be lying, and that's all that is being put to him, and he had or would have had every opportunity of dealing with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to say on this, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, do you want to ask a different question to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but I would like to put in some additional information about what's in the transcript on this, if I may. In the Milosevic transcript about what transpired because I think it pertains to some of the complaint that was made by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first reference is at page 46133 and there's been a discussion between you, Colonel, and Mr. Nice about I think the war diary. At line 19 Mr. Nice said: "You are a liar, Mr. Vukovic, and this book reveals it, doesn't it?" Your answer, line 20: "No, you're a liar, Mr. Nice." And then on the next page at line 2 Judge Robinson admonished you and said line 2: "It's not permissible to describe the Prosecutor as a liar. When he says you are a liar he does so on the basis of the evidence and its instructions, but you're not permitted to describe him as a liar. You may say he has wrong information, but don't call him a liar." And this came up again at page 46212 and Mr. Nice suggested that you were coming to court -- that you were implicated in these terrible crimes and that's why you're having to come and lie, and lie again to this court. At line 11 you said: "This is just not true and you've insulted me again, Mr. Nice, and told me that I'm lying as I've been forbidden to say that you're lying, to tell you that you're lying, then all I'm going to say is you're not telling the truth and telling untruths."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the background for this, and, Your Honour, my question regarding Mr. Nice and I think Witnesses K89 and K90 is fully supported by what he says in his statement about them. I think he's calling them liars and with regard to Merita Deda and Lizane Malaj when he denies that the crimes happened and the other things that they testified to, I think it's fair to characterize that as calling them liars as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the end of the day, Mr. Hannis, before this Tribunal is grand-standing and you have an obligation to put your case, I understand that, but it's not going to take us very far --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Then let me ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to try to ask the same thing again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask one further question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, between you and those other people I named, you're the only one that has any kind of criminal conviction involving false statements, correct? Mr. Nice doesn't and none of those other people I named have ever been convicted in court for some kind of crime involving making any false statements or causing a person to make a false statement, right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Finally I can answer. I hardly ever use the word "liar." Among my people, that is considered to be an exceptional insult --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- whoever uses that is considered to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a very uncourteous person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the witness will be allowed to answer. Please continue, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will be very brief. As I said, to say to someone that he or she is a liar or that he or she is lying is considered to be the worst insult among my people. Also, people who use that expression frequently are considered to be rather uncouth. Secondly, the assertions quoted by the honourable Prosecutor are correct, that I responded to an insult by an insult when I was reprimanded by Judge Robinson, as far as I can remember, it became clear to me that one was not allowed to do that in a court. Further on, I did not make false statements at my trial as I'm being told here by the Prosecutor. The Judge here says that I admitted to what I had done, that is to say that I did not admit to being a liar. Now, sir, since you called me a liar and I'm not allowed to call you one, I'm just going to say that what you said is not correct. And actually you know what I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I've already made it clear how the Bench here view this particular difficulty, which is one of legal culture, and we will have regard to that difference obviously when we assess what is to be drawn from these exchanges. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, could you tell us, please, who was the commander that you say ordered you to do this?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was then-Colonel Stojiljkovic, as far as I can remember. Yes, it was Colonel Stojiljkovic then. I made him aware of the problem. This shortage was there for two or three months, and then it was resolved in that way. However, in the judgement it is clearly stated that there was no crime involved in the sense of theft of fuel; rather, the fuel was used for military purposes, military needs, but it was not in accordance with the existing regulations that the documentation was done. If necessary, I can deal with this at greater length. If the entire judgement were to be read out as well as the statement of reasons, the disposition, it would be much clearer. Of course the statements too that I gave before the court that were attached to this judgement, then the matter would be perfectly clear. However, it is totally incorrect that I made false statements before a court of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not being suggested to you. What was it that Stojiljkovic told you to do?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember now, I informed him that there were these buses that the municipality had provided and we took our soldiers on these buses in order to take a bath at the common bathroom at the Lece Mine and that the military fuel that I gave to meet these needs had to be accounted for. He told me that I should divide that up in about ten travel authorisations for establishment vehicles. These were transport trucks. Actually, some of them were over 25 years old. So it is for the sake of safety of the personnel I did not use these trucks. Most of them barely made it from Djakovica to Meda [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, why didn't you tell the judge all this at the court? There's not a word of it in the judgement. I've read every word of this, not a word of it.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I said at the trial too, but I'm the one who issued the order to enter this incorrect information in the official documentation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but you told the judge that and you're saying he didn't reflect any of that, which would have been a mitigating factor in the judgement. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can state that with certainty only if you allow me to read the entire judgement, but I think there is some reference to that somewhere, and I think that my commander, after all, was aware of this too. But could I just have a look through the entire judgement because I don't know it off by heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can be sure Mr. Cepic will draw your attention to anything that he thinks contains the explanation that you're giving. Re-examination, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before he does that I have one other thing I wanted to ask you. Are you a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I still considered myself to be an officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, here I go again. Yesterday in response to Mr. Ivetic's questions pertaining to a border post, or rather, the border crossing of Cafa Prusit you gave some answers, and I need some clarifications. Could you tell me what the status of this border crossing was?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it's an official state border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember perhaps for which categories this was a border crossing?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said yesterday that when I came to the area it had been closed. As far as I can remember from my conversations with the commander of the police unit at the border, he told me that it was only pedestrians who were crossing the border there from the beginning of 1998 if I remember correctly, but I don't have any reliable information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Why was the road de-mined from Zub to Cafa Prusit?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the entire road. The entire road had not been mined in the first place, mines had not been laid along it. I think I explained that the other day. There was just this passageway that was made at the border crossing itself through an anti-personnel minefield solely in order to protect the safety of civilians who insisted to leave at this point and go to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard some testimony here by Prosecution witnesses about them crossing at that particular border crossing post. We heard that assistance was rendered in terms of food and water and that some people were provided transportation on tractors and trucks. Whose units were there in that area?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only units belonging to my unit, and at the border crossing itself there was a smallish unit, perhaps consisting of ten policemen, of the border police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Several questions were put to you in relation to the war diary. Is the war diary subjected to some verification by the superior command?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A war diary is kept in every unit and it is not been -- it is not taken for verification to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is it sent on to a higher instance?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not obligatory and it is not prescribed by the instructions or regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Down to what level of command is it necessary to keep a war diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lowest-ranking level that keeps one is the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Hannis quoted portions of the war diary in relation to Colonel Kotur, that he had seized some tools from some vehicle. What I want to know is that if Colonel Kotur as an officer was authorised to get that tool-box from that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he was authorised. I recorded that, as you know. I'm not sure why I entered this information into the war diary, of all documents, but just to prevent any misunderstanding. Colonel Kotur didn't take that tool-box for personal use. He passed it along to his driver immediately so that he could fix that military vehicle. The tool-box was under the establishment, not part and parcel of that vehicle. It was redundant, it was surplus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry to intervene. Then why was there a fuss about the tool-box when he was using it to fix his vehicle, he was there a senior person? I mean, you mentioned about it, that he took away tools, and you were cross with him. Why was this fuss?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't make a fuss about the tool-box. I wasn't cross with him about the tool-box. It's because there was this review, the quartermaster's check under the conditions that prevailed at the time. It was difficult to understand. It wasn't about the tools or about the tool-box. Truth to tell, I have no idea why I wrote that down, but as far as I remember the tool-box was surplus to requirements and it was even when it first got there because we had previously stumbled across a vehicle but we couldn't get it from Djakovica because it was out of working order. We had to leave it behind. As for these little details, I really can't tell you right now why I found that to be of importance at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What sort of an officer was Colonel Kotur?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not appropriate for a senior officer to pronounce assessments on -- for a junior officer to pronounce assessments on a senior officer. In one word he was a highly professional and hard-working officer who went about his job in a very conscientious manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis used P95 yesterday and he showed you a photograph which we -- which he claimed was a photograph of Bela Crkva. You said you couldn't be sure, so you requested another photograph with a broader view of the area. I think I could probably help with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have P95 and let's try to work with the photograph that can be found at page 11 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It can't be P95, Mr. Cepic, which is a map. Is it P93?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Probably P93.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Maybe it's my mistake. So if I can call P93, page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, perhaps I could help with this and I hope I'm not leading you. I have an impression that this photograph was taken from the north facing in a southerly direction. However, I've never been to Bela Crkva myself, just to be perfectly clear about that. There, there's some sort of a river that we can see on the far end of the photograph. Perhaps you could use that to identify this location.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I still can't really see that clearly, but if you assume that there's a bridge over that river, at the top of the photograph, and if you assume that all the way at the top of the photograph what we can see is the village of Rogovo, well in that case this might as well be Bela Crkva but I simply can't be positive about it. I crossed a section of that village. I practically skirted the village once during day-time and once during night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I want to know about the morning of the 25th, the 25th of March, and you passing through Bela Crkva. Could you please mark the route through the village that you took on that day on this photograph, if you can remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure this is the village. I'm trying to find the reference point. The Zrze-Orahovac main road should be around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Put a number 1 there, please.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then I took a turn here and this turn-off is just as you enter the village, there's a small bridge, and there's a slope leading up to trig point 460, but I have to point this out again, I'm just not certain that this is Bijela Crkva so this is all an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have an IC number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Needless to say, I took the road, but the drawing that I made is quite poor in fact. I was still driving in a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC181, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I don't know what the final explanation was, but I noticed yesterday that the witness was shown a map yesterday that had a note on it in English saying "the massacre site." As far as we've been able to gather, based on the witness's evidence, his position on that is perfectly clear. As far as I know, the witness does not, in fact, speak English; however, those markings on the map might perhaps be misleading at a later stage during the submissions by both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no suggestion that he wrote any words on any of the maps if that's what you're anxious about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no, Your Honour. The reason being I got from the Prosecution a map that was exactly the same. Mr. Sachdeva had given it to me. The P number was different but it didn't have those markings on it. I have a hard copy right in front of me. Just for that reason that I'm saying this, just to avoid any confusion, and what I'm saying, I was reluctant to disrupt the examination yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The markings are obviously things that will have been artificially put onto the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what about this action crushing the Siptar terrorist forces in the Retimlje sector? Do you know who furnished the relevant information to the command of the 549th Brigade on the way the MUP forces were deployed?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume that colleagues from the MUP did that. In this case, units were involved I think from the Djakovica MUP and the Prizren MUP. There may have been another MUP unit that was involved without me knowing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic asked you a number of questions about that. What I want to know is this: Did you submit any sort of a map to your colleagues from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and this cuts both ways: They provided none to me and I provided none to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You taught tactics, didn't you? Is it -- what is the established practice, do you mark the positions of your neighbours on a map?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We soldiers use decision we call decision maps and the neighbouring units are always marked, especially those that might in some way affect the execution of one's own unit's task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you have any influence over the planning and organization of these neighbouring forces?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have EC166 -- IC166.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And before it comes up let me ask you this: Were you subjected to any attacks from Albania in the defence sector of your battalion.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attacks were practically on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were you subjected to any attacks from behind?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were frequent attacks from behind by the Siptar terrorist groups, especially along the left wing of my unit. I know that this was also the case on several occasions with my neighbour, the 2nd Battalion of 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we have a map in front of us. What it should be about is the Reka sector south of Djakovica. Could you please draw the defence sector of your battalion on this map?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's not possible by using this map. One cannot see the defence sector of my battalion at all. We should move it eastwards so we could see Djakovica. If we do that, it just might be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps Mr. Hannis can assist me with this and give me the P number of that map that he was using yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it was P3084.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we perhaps have that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is this any help, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this one's much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis asked you to make markings on this map. What I want you to do is use a red pen if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in a little more. [In English] Could we have zoom in, please. One more time, please. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, how about now?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now we should move it further to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we don't have that much time.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, I can have a go.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Red, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That can't possibly assist because the border's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is this, what you just marked?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this is the 2nd Motorised Company. I'm sorry, it's not very neat.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This is Cafa Prusit?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you please draw a circle around that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a circle, all right. Here we find the 2nd Border Company, and then this sector over here, the Goden border post, the general sector I mean, the 3rd Motorised Company. Over here to the east, we can't see it on this map, my 1st Company near Pastrik, Mount Pastrik. There was a tank company over here minus a platoon, as far as I remember, but with a mechanised platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you use the letter T to mark that.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A capital?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, small.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was my command post. In the Zuba sector there was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: One speaker at a time, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you please put the letter K, or rather, the letter C next to your command post. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started using the Latin script just to be clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where is the command post itself, its very location?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've drawn the rocket platoon there, so it was here, around here, although it was moved at a later time, but when we say --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The sector for the entire battalion --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then Djakovica outside the line and then as far as Mount Pastrik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Get the blue pen now, please, and mark the terrorist signs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Cross-examination, Mr. Cepic? What's the issue that arose in cross-examination that you're dealing with at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, this is about Korenica and Meja, and the OTP spent quite some time on it and the witness was asked to use this map to mark the positions of those units. I think if we draw this, it might explain a number of things for the benefit of the Chamber, at least from where I stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, blue for the terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, they would most frequently emerge in these sectors, although this is not the right sector. Along the right wing there is Ljubizda where we were subjected to some attacks from and then from Brnis [phoen] but then this village should be closer to the river and then Beli Drim; it's over here, but we can't see it, from this sector here. In the Rogovo sector they would turn up on a regular basis and they were firing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you're going to have to be far more focused if there's an issue here. Korenica is miles away from what you're having drawn at the moment. This is -- I have no idea what the link of these blue marks is to the events at Korenica and Meja.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let's just focus on Reka-Korenica-Meja, were you subjected to any attacks from there; and if so, please mark them?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I for one was not subjected to any attacks, but I know that my right-hand neighbour was subjected to attacks from there, they even got as far as Babaj Boks. They crossed the river from the Reka area. They even got as far as Babaj Boks, and they were striking primarily the rear elements of the 2nd Motorised Battalion of the 125th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There's some sort of a MUP check-point that was there near Korenica, right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I get green for that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's only red, black, or blue, Mr. Cepic, like it or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Black, if it's possible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, there was an intersection here and I think it was there, but there was a permanent check-point over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please draw your own blockade line, use a dotted line, sir.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want black?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, red.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have red in that case, please. Dotted line you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how accurate I can make this. Like this, and then, as I said, over here Cabrat, perhaps like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mark the blockade line, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we know it's the dotted line, unless you're going to have another dotted line, and it includes also the part at Cabrat with which we are familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. [In English] Could we have an IC number for this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC182, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, the President of the Chamber asked you how you addressed those citizens that you were speaking to and whether you used the term of address "Siptar." You answered that you did. What I want to know now is: When you address people do you normally address them by their ethnicity: Hey you, Siptar; hey you, Turk; hey you, Serb.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly not. I'm afraid I was misunderstood when I said that. I was speaking to a person I didn't know and when doing that I address them as sir, madam. If it's someone I know, I use their name. I don't know. It was certainly not my intention for my reply to be used for this purpose and for this conclusion to be reached. I have to say this again. When I say "Siptar," I don't imply anything bad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We understand that. But you could perhaps help us by telling us in what circumstances you would address them as "Siptar"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you'll never say -- well, I don't understand what it is you're asking me. I can't approach a group of people and tell them, Hi there, Siptars. You approach them you say, Good afternoon. Those people are scared. There is absolutely no need for you to go scaring them even more, is there. I never approached --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And why would calling them "Siptars" scare them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not saying that that would scare them. I'm saying they were already considerably scared, and then the first thing you do when you talk to those people you ask them, How are you? Where are you from? Where you off to? That sort of thing. Why are you on your way there? Are you hungry? Are you thirsty? That would be my answer. I'm not sure how else to phrase this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic make-up of your subordinates, it's related to this so ...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my unit all ethnicities and national minorities from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were represented. As for my officers, I could perhaps name one for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, please don't go naming any of them. I'm just trying to speed things up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy Croat commander of the 1st Company, Bulgarian; commander of the 2nd Company, a Hungarian; commander of the 3rd Company, a Siptar; commander of the mortar company, a Gorani; commander of the anti-tank rocket platoon, a Macedonian by ethnicity. This may have been a simple coincidence in my unit, but I'm telling you what it was like. I am from Montenegro myself, come to think of it, but I don't want to be misleading the Chamber in order for someone to be a Montenegrin he must first be a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, about this judgement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you get on to that, you don't intend to try to elicit an explanation of the end of the last answer, which I for one don't understand. But if it doesn't matter, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If -- with your leave it is not so important for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Are you going to finish before we break? Is this your objective?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I just have couple questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's try and do that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Could we have P3083, please. Page 100 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, please, could you have a look on the last page, this gives the reasons for the conviction. Could you please read out the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth line, the sentence starts with the following words: "Bearing in mind ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to claim a fault in the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's no need for it to be read out. We've got it in front of us. Some of us have hard copies. Please proceed to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was this fuel used for, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fuel was used for the soldiers of my unit to take a bath --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know the answer, that it was to use buses to get them to the baths. Let's ask something we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel what were your official marks or grades?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first official one was good, later on very good, and all the rest were excellent, including outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any decorations while in active duty?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How many times and what for?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times, although I personally recognise only the last order that was bestowed upon me because it was given in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure how this arises out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It could go to credibility bearing in mind your accusation, Mr. Hannis, then it's clearly a possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, many a brave man can be a liar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, but many a man could be convicted on the basis of an explanation he gave himself rather than on the basis of misleading a court. So what's good for the goose is good for the gander. Please continue, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, just very quickly, what was it that this decoration was bestowed on you for?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For merit in defending the fatherland.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Before that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previously the explanation provided was for conscientiously carrying out my military duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, before you proceed, Mr. Cepic, could I find out when he got decorated for merit in defending the fatherland and also the following one, when it was. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last decoration which I said that I found dearest to my heart was the month of August or September 1999. Earlier on this took place several times. The previous one I got in the military academy sometime in 1993/1994, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was the decoration that you've referred to in August or September 1999 one that was issued to large numbers of the VJ who participated in the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you a definite answer because I was not the one handing out the decorations, but it is called a decoration for merit in defending the fatherland and it is of the first degree, either the fatherland or the country, please don't take my word for it, but I assume that there weren't very many such decorations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And my last question: Colonel, were you ever promoted along the fast track during your career?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice, from major to lieutenant-colonel and from lieutenant-colonel to colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, this is a question that perhaps you can assist us with, bearing in mind the legal culture issue that we were looking at earlier. Is there a Serb expression that's equivalent to "liar" in English where someone is obviously misleading in an important area, giving untrue evidence in an important matter, what word would you use in Serb to describe such a person?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, one would say one does not speak the truth. From my experience in the judiciary - and I did not appear only before Serbian courts but also in courts in the neighbouring countries - the word "liar" was never used. From the point of view of culture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the point of view of culture, the word "liar" is extremely offensive in ordinary communication, everyday communication; and in judicial practice it is not used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a word that liar translates into in Serb?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Lazov."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So do we take from that, Mr. Cepic, that there's no polite word for a liar that you would use in a formal context, either in the court or some other formal environment?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the impression that my colleague Mr. Fila wants to give an explanation for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the question is of a verbal nature. In our language if you say to someone that he or she lied before a court of law, that has to be read out in your judgement; and then you can speak of false testimony, as in perjury. Until then you can just say to this person, You are not saying the truth, but you cannot tell a person, You're lying. This whole story with Mr. Hannis, who's upset for nothing and we're all upset for nothing and it's all on account of this one single word. In our system you're not allowed to say to anyone that he or she is a liar until you have a judgement from a court of law corroborating that. Until then you say that they do not speak the truth. Now, if you convict me of having spoken falsely before this court of law, then you can call me a liar if there's a judgement saying that, whereas this way I can just say to someone, You're not telling the truth. You never tell the truth, I can even say that, but I can't say you're lying. Now, I don't know what the difference is. I have no idea, but I guess it has to do with sensitivity of a people, of a nation, especially when we're talking about a small people, a small nation. I think that would be the explanation. I'm sorry, I just wanted to help you. That's the whole story, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So that's the Serbian history of sophisticated people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we're small and oversensitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one sentence in addition to what Mr. Fila said. Most of the cases before courts in Belgrade have to do with people charging other people that they were not telling the truth, so it's about libel and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say that I hadn't noted in particular that anything had upset Mr. Hannis or anyone else in particular. I thought that we were simply clearing the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I inquire, Your Honour, in the future should I then say, You're an unconvicted liar? Would that perhaps work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you can reflect on how to deal with this should it arise again. Mr. Vukovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give evidence. I know that you've been anxious to say a lot more than perhaps you feel you've been given an opportunity to say. The way this system operates, as you know from your last visit and this one, is that the counsel on both sides have every opportunity to ask the questions they feel it is appropriate to ask and to give you an opportunity to explain what they think is relevant and what you ought to be given an opportunity to explain. As far as I'm concerned and the rest of the Bench, that is what has happened here. You have been given every opportunity to explain all that the parties considered it was appropriate for you to deal with, so thank you for that. You are now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it the next witness is Mihajlo Gergar?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think he should be in place when we resume at 20 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gergar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll now be examined by Mr. Cepic on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the Defence team of General Vladimir Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: For the transcript would you give me your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: I am Mihajlo Gergar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Let us now go back to this statement. If I were to put the same questions to you today that were put at the time when this statement was given, would you give the stadium answers?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a copy of the statement given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, is that the statement?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could it please be admitted into evidence, Gergar Mihajlo's witness statement, number 5D1400.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you have a lot of military experience. I would be interested in the following: Can the population, the unarmed population, be used in the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of the Law on Defence, non-mobilised population during a war situation can be assigned patrol duty, guard duty, or they can be assigned to civil defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look at P985, which is the Law on Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While the document is coming up, if I may, I'm wondering if the record at 42, 11 -- 42, 15, is correct. The question seems -- I don't know if the question in Serbian and what the witness heard in Serbian is what is translated there. Can the unarmed population be used in the defence of the country. I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I assume the question has been properly translated. No one's suggested otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One thing that's not clear to me is what position Mr. Gergar held during 1999. I don't think that the statement tells us that, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in 1999, what position were you in?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: In 1999 I was commander of the 211th Armoured Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Article 61 on our screens of this particular law. In Serbian it should be the second or third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Does this legal provision confirm what was stated previously, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: Yes. Article 61 says that in a state of war, and if necessary, in case of an imminent threat of war the local population may organize guards, patrols, and civil defence units to protect the civilian population and property from attacks."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me who takes the decision to set up such units and who commands such units?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: Such units are established in accordance with the decision made by state organs. Such units are commanded by state organs. In certain situations battalion commanders and artillery battalion commanders can issue assignments to such units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Articles 62 and 63 displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Actually, let's just have a look at this last sentence here. You said state organs on the basis of decisions made by state organs, can you see it spelled out precisely here, can you see it, or can you tell us without looking at the document what state organ establishes such units?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look at the next page, Articles 62 and 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Tell me, we see what is written here. Were such units resubordinated to you or to the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: Such units were not resubordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now I would be interested in a theoretical question. If enemy forces, terrorist forces, are fortified in a built-up area, in accordance with the rules of the Army of Yugoslavia, is the use of tanks allowed?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How is that regulated, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: This is regulated in our combat and tactical rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 5D1255.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the other page in English, could you please tell us what kind of rule this is.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: This is a rule of infantry mountain alpine company platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see item 253. In B/C/S it is -- in e-court it should be page 47, actually; and in English I think it's the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, item 253 from the mentioned rules, or rather, the last paragraph, does that corroborate what you just said?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: Yes. Item 253 confirms my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us in the briefest possible terms, you're an experienced tank man, what is the use of these tanks imply, the use of one or two tanks - guns or cannons?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: The combat order of a company for attacking a built-up area involves the establishment or one or two assault groups, and usually along with the pioneers and marksmen there are one or two tanks or cannons that are given to such a unit for support to the subgroup that is to attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There may be something wrong with this translation, Mr. Cepic, but I don't see the bit in English that you're referring to, and I see that different paragraphs have been translated -- or at least different paragraphs appear on the left and on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, yes, my colleagues are telling me too that in the Serbian language 253 ends and continues -- and continues on the next page; and we, in order not to translate the entire book, translated only those parts that we thought were relevant for our defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell me where in the English in 253 I see the corroboration for the use of tanks against fortifications in built-up areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this. If you look at the second paragraph of 253, the use of two tanks, one or two tanks or guns is allowed. Before that it states that a combat group taking bunkers and fortified buildings in the company can set up one to two assault groups for clearing up -- one to two assault groups and one group for the purpose of clearing up. If necessary, perhaps can witness -- perhaps the witness can read this for the sake of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I see what you're referring to now. It's the translation of the question said it was the last paragraph of 253, but I see where it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we've now looked at the rule. Let us move on to a different topic. When was the brigade resubordinated to the corps?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: The brigade itself was resubordinated to the Pristina Corps 29th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We looked a while ago at that rule allowing the use of armoured vehicles and tanks. Did you actually do that? Did you use tanks?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: No, we did not use tanks to attack any populated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: We didn't use tanks to attack populated areas primarily in order to avoid inflicting major losses on the population and material goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Colonel, the brigade or you as its commander, did you ever issue an order to defend?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: Yes, I issued an order to defend to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please on our screens see Defence Exhibit 5D587.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is this the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR
utterances.text: Yes, this is the order to defend.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
